title: Henry Ford's Five Dollar Day
text:
By 1913 Ford's Highland Park plant near Detroit was running the new moving assembly line, and the work was fast, repetitive and exhausting. Workers quit in huge numbers. The company had to hire several times its workforce each year to keep the line staffed, and every new man had to be trained.

On 5 January 1914 Henry Ford and his business manager James Couzens announced a plan that shocked industry: a minimum of five dollars for an eight-hour day, roughly double the usual wage for such work, paid as a share of profits to qualifying workers. The next day thousands of men gathered at the plant gates in the winter cold hoping to be hired, and on one day the crowd grew so large that police turned fire hoses on it.

The extra pay came with conditions. To qualify, workers had to meet standards of conduct and home life checked by the company's Sociological Department, a paternalism many found intrusive. But turnover fell sharply and productivity rose. Ford later wrote in My Life and Work that paying five dollars a day for an eight-hour day was one of the finest cost-cutting moves the company ever made. Better-paid workers could also afford to buy the cars they built, which Ford liked to point out.
lesson: Paying people well can be a strategy rather than a cost, if it reduces turnover and raises commitment. Count the hidden expense of constantly replacing people.
source: Henry Ford with Samuel Crowther, My Life and Work (1922), chapter 10; contemporary press reports
